ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *-ōder. Proto-Indo-European *-Hōder.? Latin -ō Late Latin pedōnem Old French peon Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -ārius Old French -ier Old French peonier Middle French pionnierder. English pioneer From Middle French pionnier (“originally, a foot soldier”), Old French peonier, from peon (“a foot soldier”) (modern French: pion). See pawn (in chess).

senses.d: One who goes before, as into the wilderness, preparing the way for others to follow.
A person or other entity who is first or among the earliest in any field of inquiry, enterprise, or progress.
ex: Some people will consider their national heroes to be pioneers of civilization.
Certain politicians can be considered as pioneers of reform.

senses.d: A soldier detailed or employed to form roads, dig trenches, and make bridges, as an army advances; a sapper.
A member of any of several European organizations advocating abstinence from alcohol.
A member of a children’s organization operated by the Communist Party, typically in the second of three stages toward becoming a member of the Party itself.
To be the first to do or achieve (something), preparing the way for others to follow.
ex: The young doctor pioneered a new life-saving surgical technique.

grp.label: member of a child organization in the Soviet bloc

senses.d: Involving accomplishments or activities that have not been done before, or developing or using new methods or techniques.
ex: Norway as a polar nation would not have been what it is today without their tireless pioneering efforts.

senses.d: The activity of the verb pioneer.
A scoutcraft skill that involves building structures using staves and knots.
